name: Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder)
summary: Painful progressive restriction of active and passive glenohumeral movement, typically with external rotation most limited.

looksLike: Difficulty dressing, reaching behind back or overhead
redFlags: Acute traumatic inability to elevate arm
Fever, hot swollen joint or systemic illness
Cancer history, unexplained mass or constitutional symptoms
firstSteps: Education about variable natural history and symptom-guided activity
Maintain tolerable movement; avoid forceful stretching during highly irritable phase
Coordinate medical management of pain and relevant metabolic conditions

assess: Global active and passive ROM restriction
Capsular-pattern loss of active and passive ROM

tests.name: Passive External Rotation Assessment
tests.purpose: Identify the characteristic global capsular restriction pattern.
tests.positive: Marked restriction compared with other side with a firm capsular end-feel and concordant symptoms.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Education about variable natural history and symptom-guided activity
Maintain tolerable movement; avoid forceful stretching during highly irritable phase
Coordinate medical management of pain and relevant metabolic conditions
dose: Gentle assisted ROM: 5–10 reps, several times/day, within tolerable pain
Pendulum or supported table slides if comfortable
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Progress capsular mobility within irritability limits
Restore rotator cuff and scapular strength as ROM allows
Functional reaching and behind-back tasks graded gradually
dose: Low-load prolonged stretch: 20–60 seconds, 3–5 reps when irritability permits
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Increase overhead, dressing and occupational capacity
dose: Task-specific reaching practice with gradual range/load increase
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: ROM adequate for work and daily tasks
Strength and activity tolerance restored without prolonged flare

logic: Match treatment intensity to irritability. A very painful shoulder often needs gentle movement, not aggressive stretching.
Expect recovery to be gradual. The goal is steady improvement in function and sleep, not forcing normal range in one session.
Differentiate true capsular restriction from rotator-cuff pain, arthritis or neurological disease.
structures: Glenohumeral capsule and rotator interval; capsular fibrosis and synovial changes are implicated.
mechanism: Often gradual onset without a single injury
Associated with diabetes and thyroid disease; may follow immobilisation
classification: Thawing/recovery phase; stages overlap and duration varies
investigations: Diagnosis is usually clinical; radiographs may help exclude glenohumeral arthritis when indicated.
Ultrasound/MRI is not routinely required for a typical presentation.
manual: Low-grade mobilization may be appropriate in painful/high-irritability stage; stronger mobilization only when irritability is lower.
Manual therapy is adjunctive and should not provoke prolonged flare.
Gentle glenohumeral mobilization in highly irritable stage
Progressive posterior/inferior/anterior glides when stiffness dominates and irritability allows
High irritability: Grade I–II glenohumeral mobilization for pain modulation.
Lower irritability/stiffness dominant: progress posterior/inferior/anterior glides with careful reassessment.
Scapulothoracic mobilization can be added if it improves functional reach.
modalities: Heat before mobility may help comfort.
Discuss medical options such as intra-articular corticosteroid with the treating prescriber when pain limits rehabilitation; physiotherapists should not independently prescribe.
Heat before mobility may improve comfort
TENS can be considered for pain
Heat 10–15 minutes before mobility if helpful.
TENS can be used short term for pain.
dosing: Pendulum or relaxed movement: 30–60 seconds × 2–3 bouts.
Assisted flexion/external rotation: 5–10 slow reps, several times/day.
Low-load stretching: 20–30 seconds × 3–5 reps when irritability allows.
progression: Increase stretch duration and load as irritability decreases
Increase stretch intensity only when post-treatment flare is small and short-lived.
Progress from assisted to active motion, then resistance and overhead function.
If progress is very limited with severe pain, coordinate medical options such as injection when appropriate.
mistakes: Aggressive stretching in a highly painful shoulder
Assuming every stiff shoulder is adhesive capsulitis
Aggressive end-range mobilization in the painful stage.
Forcing through severe pain because the shoulder is stiff.
pearls: Passive external rotation loss is a key clinical clue.
Stage and irritability should guide exercise and mobilization intensity.
education: Explain the slow natural course in simple language.
Encourage frequent gentle movement rather than rare aggressive stretching.
escalation: Medical review for severe persistent pain, diagnostic uncertainty or consideration of injection/hydrodilatation/surgical options

tests.name: Passive External Rotation Assessment
tests.purpose: Identify the characteristic global capsular restriction pattern.
tests.positive: Marked restriction compared with other side with a firm capsular end-feel and concordant symptoms.
tests.patientPosition: Supine or seated; stabilise scapula and gently assess passive external rotation with arm by side.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Supports adhesive capsulitis when global passive restriction and history fit; exclude arthritis and other causes.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
